Thanks for the call this morning. Per our internal follow-up, we pushed an export of our traffic profile and three representative model configs (short-chat, long-context summarization, and an embedding service) — attaching the CSV. Our primary asks: predictable 99th percentile latency under 400ms for chat (short), capacity to support 800 concurrent embedding requests, and a cost target that keeps our month-to-month spend predictable for Q4.

Quick question: you mentioned Redwood can do mixed SKU pools and automatic fallbacks. For budget reasons we prefer to avoid H100 for the whole fleet; is a hybrid H100+A100+L4 approach realistic for Delphic, or would you recommend a conservative A100-first approach? We also have concerns about memory-heavy summarization (8k-32k context).

Appreciate a short note with tradeoffs so we can present to finance tomorrow morning.

Best,

From: aisha_rahman@redwood.ai
To: Elena Morales <elena@delphic.ai>
Cc: ops@delphic.ai, kimberly_park@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: Delphic Dedicated: GPU guardrails & SKU-fit recommendation

Elena — thanks for the profile. I reviewed the CSV and sketched an ops-friendly recommendation below. High level: hybrid pool makes sense, but with clear guardrails per workload to hit both latency and cost targets.

Summary recommendation (short):
- Embeddings: L4-backed autoscaled pool for high concurrency; use batching + small model quant (4-bit) to hit tokens/$ targets. Reserve baseline slots to guarantee throughput.
- Short-chat (low-latency): A100 80% of steady-state capacity; tune low-concurrency lanes (smaller batch windows) to meet 99p latency. Use prefix caching for repeated prompts.
- Long-context summarization (8k–32k): H100 for the tail of long-context jobs and A100 for mid-range; prioritize H100 only for pinned long-context heavy variant to keep costs down.

Tradeoffs / rationale:
- Memory: L4 has limited VRAM; excellent for embeddings and small models but will OOM on >16k context unless segmented/chunked. H100 gives headroom for 32k+ and large-batch KV cache; A100 is the best price/perf sweet spot for 4k–16k.
- Latency: A100 typically wins on steady short-chat 99p when configured with smaller batch windows and prewarming; H100 reduces latency for very large attention windows. L4 excels at parallel small requests but introduces variability with batching.
- Cost: H100 unit price 2–3x A100; guardrail = only route long-context heavy requests (where memory matters) to H100 and failover to A100 degraded-mode when latency budget allows. L4 for embeddings unlocks large concurrency with lower cost.

Operational notes:
- Autoscaling policy: baseline reserved slots (70% of expected steady-state) + burst pool. This prevents noisy neighbor impacts and keeps 99p stable.
- Fallback policy: rank by memory fit -> latency SLO -> cost. e.g., prefer A100 when memory fits; if A100 saturated, route to L4 (if model quantized/chunked) with explicit degraded-latency flag.
- Monitoring: add prompt-level SLOs and a daily mismatch alert when quality regresses after quantization.

I've cc'd Kimberly to run numbers against our Q3 SKU cost sheet and Dev to validate the fallback feasibility with current runtime kernels. Sending a proposed cost spreadsheet next.

—Aisha
Sr. Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachment: SKU_cost_estimate_Q3.xlsx (XLSX, 110KB)

Quick internal note (forwarding to Elena with numbers aside):

A few concrete knobs to present to finance:
1) Slot sizing: recommend 1.25x steady-state reservation on A100 to preserve headroom for 99p spikes. That means reserved A100 slots = round_up(0.8 * peak_short_chat_capacity * 1.25).
2) H100 carve-out: cap at <=15% of total reserved compute unless Delphic commits to a 12-month reserved block — otherwise use burst credits for H100.
3) L4 pool concurrency: target 800 concurrent embeddings by using 24 L4 cards across 3 nodes with batch windows tuned to 10–30ms; use token pooling for short inference calls.
4) Quantization policy: allow 4-bit for embeddings and short-chat (with evaluation gate), force 8-bit or fp16 for long-context summarization unless customer consents to quality risk.

Dev — can you confirm the runtime will support automatic reroute to A100-degraded with a "degraded_latency" response header so Delphic can decide to show a spinner or degrade quality on the client? If yes, we'll include that as part of the SLA carve-out.

—Kimberly (RevOps)

From: dev_patel@redwood.ai
To: aisha_rahman@redwood.ai, kimberly_park@redwood.ai, Elena Morales <elena@delphic.ai>
Date: 2026-09-06T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Delphic Dedicated: GPU guardrails & SKU-fit recommendation

Elena / team — quick confirmation from infra/runtime:

- We already expose a "route_score" decision policy in the control plane that can route by memory fit and latency headroom. We can add a response header "x-redwood-fallback" with values (none | a100-degraded | l4-quant) so the client can treat fallback events. Implementation ETA: 2 weeks for the header and dashboard telemetry; 4 weeks for a canary rollout.
- Automatic chunking for 32k+ summarization: we have a streaming-chunk helper but it requires an evaluation step to validate output quality for Delphic models. If they want seamless H100 behavior, we'll need the H100 carve-out described by Kimberly.
- Cost gating: we can enforce routing limits by daily spend thresholds and auto-rollback to cheaper pool when projected spend > threshold; this is supported via our billing integrations.

Next steps proposed:
1) Approve the high-level hybrid approach (L4 for embeddings, A100 for short-chat, H100 reserved for long-context tail).
2) Sign a 12-month reserve for H100 carve-out >= 10% of committed compute to get a meaningful unit discount.
3) Run a 2-week evaluation: enable 4-bit quant for embeddings and short-chat on a canary subset (5% traffic) and collect quality/latency telemetry.

Elena — if you approve, we'll deliver a short commercial term sheet with reserve options and a technical runbook for the canary.

Thanks,
Dev
Platform Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
